blocks.text: Whose size is immense, so that on its broad back it could carry a newborn boy. Pliny: They exceed the height of a horseman sitting on a horse. Albertus: The ostrich is about five or six feet tall from the feet to the back; it has a very long neck, etc. Therefore the Arabs call it هيق [hayq] heic and هيقم [hayqam] heicam from the length of its neck, and اسقف [usquf] ascaph from its height. This is also what they call the bishops of the Christians, but there the word is derived from the Greek. And of a plant, استرال [istarāl] isterala means to grow tall like the chick of an ostrich, which in Arabic is called رال [rāl] raal. [II, 869] The ostrich, then, raising itself so high, laughs at the horse and its rider. [col. 262] Laughs, that is, scorns, as the Greek Scholiast has it: Καταφρονοῦσα ἵππου σὺν τῷ ἀναβάτῃ διὰ τὴν ἰσχὺν, ὥς φασι, καὶ τὸ μέγεθος [kataphronousa hippou syn tō anabatē dia tēn ischyn, hōs phasi, kai to megethos]. Despising the horse with its rider, on account of its strength, as they say, and its size. Rightly, except that the ostrich should have been said to scorn horse and horseman not in reliance on its strength but on its speed. Hence Pliny: They exceed the height of a horseman sitting on a horse, and surpass him in speed. And Xenophon, in book 1 of the Anabasis, says that the horsemen of Cyrus caught wild asses and roe deer in Arabia, but could in no way overtake the ostriches: Στρουθὸν δὲ οὐδεὶς ἔλαβεν· οἱ δὲ διώξαντες τῶν ἱππέων ταχὺ ἐπαύοντο· πολὺ γὰρ ἀπέσπα αποφεύγουσα [strouthon de oudeis elaben; hoi de diōxantes tōn hippeōn tachy epauonto; poly gar apespa apopheugousa]. No one caught an ostrich; and those who pursued it soon gave up, for in its flight it drew far ahead. This is remarkable in an army equipped with many thousands of horsemen. It is said, indeed, that in Africa, among the breed of horses called Arabian, some are found that can overtake an ostrich in running, but very few, and these of immense price. Marmol, book 1, chapter 23: Cavallos Barbaros son llamados en toda Europa los, que vienen de Berberia: mas ay una especie de cavallos en Africa, y en Egypto, y en las Arabias, y en toda Asia, que llaman cavallos Arabes, que son de casta de cavallos salvages, que se crian por los desiertos de Arabia, etc. Son est rañamente ligeros, y la mayor experiencia, que se haze de su ligereza es quando alcançan una fiera llamada Lamte, o a un abestruz. Porque este tal cavallos es apreciado en mil ducados de oro, o en cien camellos. Mas ay pocos dellos en Berberia. That is: Throughout Europe the horses brought from Barbary are called Barbary horses; but in Africa, Egypt, Arabia and all Asia there is a breed of horses which they call Arabian, descended from those bred in the deserts of Arabia, etc. They are wonderfully swift, and there is no greater proof of their speed than when they overtake the wild beast called the Lamte, or an ostrich. Therefore such a horse is valued at a thousand gold ducats, or a hundred camels. But in Barbary there are few such. And certainly this is the common opinion of the Arabs, that there is no animal which surpasses the ostrich in running. On this point these words of Alkazuinius are explicit: لا يصبقها شي من الحيوانات [lā yaṣbiquhā shay min al-ḥayawānāt] None of the animals outruns it. How this comes about we have shown above ^{f)}: that, using its wings as a sail, it swims, as it were, in the air. Hence Oppian, Cynegetica book 3, verse 500:
Ἠέρος ὑψιπόροισιν ἐπιπλώουσι κελεύθοις, [Ēeros hypsiporoisin epiplōousi keleuthois,]
They swim along the lofty paths of the air. And shortly after, [II, 870] Αὐτοῖσιν φορέουσιν ἴσον τάχος οἰωνοῖσιν, [Autoisin phoreousin ison tachos oiōnoisin,]

They are of equal speed with the birds themselves. Accordingly the Arabs coined many words to express this. Thus of the ostrich, زازا [zāzā] zaza means to flow rather than walk, with head, wings and tail raised; رفرف [rafrafa] raphrapha, to run while flapping the wings, like the Talmudic רפרף riphreph; كحص [kaḥaṣa] chahatsa, to go so swiftly as almost to escape the sight. And for this very reason the ostrich is called عصوف [ʿaṣūf], that is, whirlwind, and by other names, at least ten, derived from the rapidity of its running ^{(6)}. Indeed it spurs itself on to run with certain bony spikes which lie hidden under its wings and serve it as spurs. On these it would be easy to adduce much more; but to set this out point by point is not the business of the present place, and it is enough for us to have explained the meaning of the Sacred Writer.
